doc_description: This document provides a comprehensive overview of the World Health Organization's 2023 Model List of Essential Medicines, detailing guidelines, categories, and specific medications essential for various health conditions, emphasizing their formulations, dosages, and therapeutic alternatives to ensure effective healthcare delivery.

structure.title: Preface
structure.summary: The partial document outlines the World Health Organization's (WHO) guidelines and licensing information regarding the Model List of Essential Medicines for 2023. It emphasizes the importance of proper citation and the non-commercial use of the work under a Creative Commons license. The document details the structure of the Essential Medicines List, including a core list of essential medicines for basic healthcare needs and a complementary list for priority diseases requiring specialized care. It explains the significance of symbols used in the list, such as those indicating restrictions for children or the need for specialist facilities. Additionally, it highlights the responsibility of national authorities to ensure the pharmaceutical quality of listed medicines and provides resources for further information on quality assurance and treatment guidelines. The document also includes disclaimers regarding the interpretation and use of the material, as well as the non-endorsement of specific products or companies by WHO.

  WHO Model List of Essential Medicines – 23rd List (2023) 
Explanatory notes  
The core list presents a list of minimum medicine needs for a basic health -care system, listing the most efficacious, safe and 
cost–effective medicines for priority conditions. Priority conditions are selected on the basis of current and estimated future 
public health relevance, and potential for safe and cost -effective treatment.  
 
Where the [c] symbol is placed next to an individual medicine or strength of medicine on the core list it signifies that there is 
a specific indication for restricting its use to children.  
 
The complementary  list presents essential medicines for priority diseases, for which specialized diagnostic or monitoring 
facilities, and/or specialist medical care, and/or specialist training are needed. In case of doubt medicines may also be lis ted 
as co mplementary on the basis of consistent higher costs or less attractive cost -effectiveness in a variety of settings.  
 
Where the  [c] symbol is placed next to an individual medicine or strength of medicine on the complementary list it signifies 
that the medi cine(s) require(s) specialist diagnostic or monitoring facilities, and/or specialist medical care, and/or specialist 
training for their use in children.  
 
The square box  symbol () is intended to indicate therapeutic alternatives to the listed medicine that  may be considered for 
selection in national essential medicines lists. Alternatives may be individual medicines, or multiple medicines within a 
pharmacological class or chemical  subgroup, defined at the 4th level of the Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical (ATC) 
classification , which have similar clinical effectiveness and safety.  The listed medicine should be the example of the clas s or 
subgroup for which there is the best evidence for effectiveness and safety. In some cases, this may be the first medicine 
that is licensed for marketing; in other instances, subsequently licensed compounds may be safer or more effective. Where 
there i s no difference in terms of efficacy and safety data, the listed medicine should be the one that is generally available at 
the lowest price, based on international drug price information sources. Not all square box listings are applicable to medicine 
selec tion for children.  A square box is not used to indicate alternative generic brands of the same small molecule medicines, 
nor alternative biosimilars of biological medicines. However, the selection and use of quality -assured generics and biosimilars 
of esse ntial medicines at country level is recommended.  
 
National lists should not use a similar symbol and should be specific in their final selection, which would depend on local 
availability and price.  
 
The a symbol indicates that there is an age or weight re striction on use of the medicine; details for each medicine can be 
found in Table 1.1.  
 
The presence of an entry on the Essential Medicines List carries no assurance as to pharmaceutical quality. It is the 
responsibility of the relevant national or regional drug regulatory authority to ensure that each product is of appropriate 
pharmaceutical quality (including stability) and that, when relevant, different products are interchangeable.  
 
For recommendations and advice concerning all aspects of the qua lity assurance of medicines see the WHO website 
https://www.who.int/teams/health -product -and-policy -standards/standards -and-specifications/norms -and-standar ds-for-
pharmaceuticals/guidelines/quality -assurance   
 
Medicines and dosage forms are listed in alphabetical order within each section and the order of listing does not imply 
preference for one form over another. Standard treatment guidelines should be cons ulted for information on appropriate 
dosage forms.  
 
The main terms used for dosage forms in the Essential Medicines List can be found in Table 1.2.  
 
Definitions of many of these terms and pharmaceutical quality requirements applicable to the different categories are 
published in the current edition of The International Pharmacopoeia . https://www.who.int/teams/health -product -and-policy -
standards/standards -and-specifications/norms -and-standards -for-pharmaceuticals/pharmacopoeia .

structure.title: WHO Model List of Essential Medicines – 23rd List (2023)
structure.summary: The partial document outlines the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines for 2023, detailing the core and complementary lists of essential medicines necessary for a basic healthcare system. The core list identifies the most effective, safe, and cost-efficient medicines for priority health conditions, while the complementary list includes medicines requiring specialized care or training. Symbols are used to indicate specific uses, such as the [c] symbol for pediatric use and the square box () for therapeutic alternatives. The document emphasizes the importance of local selection based on availability and pricing, and it clarifies that inclusion on the list does not guarantee pharmaceutical quality, which is the responsibility of national regulatory authorities. Additionally, it provides guidance on dosage forms and references to further quality assurance resources. The document also includes a section listing various anesthetics and preoperative medications, specifying their forms and therapeutic alternatives.

nodes.title: ANAESTHETICS, PREOPERATIVE MEDICINES AND MEDICAL GASES
nodes.summary: The partial document outlines the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines for 2023, specifically focusing on the category of anaesthetics, preoperative medicines, and medical gases. It details various general anaesthetics, including inhalational and injectable forms, such as halothane, isoflurane, nitrous oxide, and ketamine, along with their respective formulations. The document also covers local anaesthetics like bupivacaine and lidocaine, providing information on their injectable forms and concentrations. Additionally, it includes preoperative medications and sedation options for short-term procedures, highlighting drugs such as atropine, midazolam, and morphine, along with their available formulations. The document emphasizes the importance of these essential medicines in medical practice.

nodes.title: Preoperative medication and sedation for short-term procedures
nodes.summary: The partial document outlines the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines for 2023, specifically focusing on anaesthetics, preoperative medicines, medical gases, and medicines for pain and palliative care. It details various categories of anaesthetics, including general and local anaesthetics, injectable and inhalational forms, along with their therapeutic alternatives. The document also covers preoperative medications and sedation options, highlighting specific drugs like atropine and midazolam. Additionally, it discusses medical gases, particularly oxygen, and their applications in managing hypoxaemia. In the section on pain management, the document lists non-opioid analgesics, such as acetylsalicylic acid, ibuprofen, and paracetamol, along with opioid analgesics like codeine, fentanyl, and morphine, including their formulations and recommended uses. The document emphasizes the importance of these medicines in clinical practice, particularly for pain relief and palliative care.

nodes.title: Antibacterials
nodes.summary:
The partial document outlines the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines for 2023, specifically focusing on the classification of antibiotics into three groups: Access, Watch, and Reserve. 

1. **Access Group Antibiotics**: These antibiotics are essential for treating common infections and have a lower potential for resistance. They are recommended as first or second choice treatments for various infectious syndromes and should be widely available and affordable.

2. **Watch Group Antibiotics**: This group includes antibiotics with a higher risk of resistance and is prioritized for stewardship programs. They are recommended for specific infections and require careful monitoring to prevent resistance.

3. **Reserve Group Antibiotics**: These are last-resort options for treating infections caused by multi-drug-resistant organisms. Their use should be limited to specific cases where other treatments have failed, and they are subject to strict stewardship measures to maintain their effectiveness.

The document also provides specific examples of antibiotics within the Access group, detailing their formulations and recommended uses for various medical conditions, emphasizing the importance of appropriate antibiotic use to combat antimicrobial resistance.
nodes.text:
WHO Model List of Essential Medicines  – 23rd List (202 3)  
 WHO Model List of Essential Medicines – 23rd List (2023) page 8 6.2 Antibacterials  
To assist in the development of tools for antibiotic stewardship at local, national  and global levels and to reduce 
antimicrobial resistance, the Access, Watch, Reserve (AWaRe) classification of antibiotics was developed – where 
antibiotics are classified into different groups to emphasize the importance of their appropriate use.  
ACCESS GROUP ANTIBIOTICS  
This group includes antibiotics that have activity against a wide range of commonly encountered susceptible pathogens 
while also showing lower resistance potential than antibiotics in the other groups. Selected Access group antibiotics a re 
recommended as essential first or second choice empiric treatment options for infectious syndromes reviewed by the 
EML Expert Committee and are listed as individual medicines on the Model Lists to improve access and promote 
appropriate use.  They are ess ential antibiotics that should be widely available, affordable and quality assured.  
 
WATCH GROUP ANTIBIOTICS  
This group includes antibiotic classes that have higher resistance potential and includes most of the highest priority agents  
among the Critically Important Antimicrobials for Human Medicine  and/or antibiotics that are at relatively high risk of 
selection of bacterial resistance.  These medicines should be prioritized as key targets of stewardship programs and 
monitoring. Selected Watch group antibiotics are recommended as essential first or secon d choice empiric treatment 
options for a limited number of specific infectious syndromes and are listed as individual medicines on the Model Lists.  
RESERVE GROUP ANTIBIOTICS  
This group includes antibiotics and antibiotic classes that should be reserved fo r treatment of confirmed or suspected 
infections due to multi -drug -resistant organisms.  Reserve group antibiotics should be treated as “last resort” options. 
Selected Reserve group antibiotics are listed as individual medicines on the Model Lists when they  have a favourable risk -
benefit profile and proven activity against “Critical Priority” or “High Priority” pathogens identified by the WHO Priority 
Pathogens List , notably carbapenem resistant Enterobacteriaceae . These antibiotics should be accessible, but their use 
should be tailored to highly specific patients and settings, when all alternatives have failed or are not suitable.  These 
medicines could be protected and prioritized as key targets of national and international stewardship programs involving 
monitoring and utilization reporting, to preserve their effectiveness.

nodes.title: Reserve group antibiotics
nodes.summary:
The partial document outlines the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines for 2023, focusing on various antibiotics, antileprosy, antituberculosis, and antifungal medicines. It specifies the formulations, dosages, and recommended uses for each medication. Key points include:

1. **Antibiotics**: 
   - Piperacillin + tazobactam is highlighted as a first-choice treatment for severe complicated intraabdominal infections, high-risk febrile neutropenia, hospital-acquired pneumonia, and necrotizing fasciitis.
   - Vancomycin is recommended for C. difficile infections and as a second choice for other conditions.
   - Meropenem is preferred for acute bacterial meningitis in neonates and complicated infections.

2. **Reserve Group Antibiotics**: 
   - Includes cefiderocol, ceftazidime + avibactam, and colistin, among others, with specific indications for use in specialized settings.

3. **Antileprosy Medicines**: 
   - Emphasizes the importance of combination therapy to prevent drug resistance, listing medications like clofazimine, dapsone, and rifampicin.

4. **Antituberculosis Medicines**: 
   - Recommends fixed-dose combinations and highlights various drugs such as isoniazid, rifampicin, and moxifloxacin for treating tuberculosis, including multidrug-resistant strains.

5. **Antifungal Medicines**: 
   - Lists essential antifungals like amphotericin B, fluconazole, and itraconazole, noting their specific uses and formulations.

Overall, the document serves as a comprehensive guide for healthcare providers on essential medicines, their applications, and the importance of adherence to WHO standards for treatment.

The partial document outlines the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines for 2023, focusing on various categories of medicines essential for treating HIV, hepatitis, and other viral infections. Key points include:

1. **Integrase Inhibitors**: Details on specific integrase inhibitors like dolutegravir and raltegravir, including their formulations and indications for use, particularly in pregnant women and second-line regimens.

2. **Fixed-Dose Combinations**: Information on combinations of antiretroviral medicines, such as abacavir + lamivudine and dolutegravir + lamivudine + tenofovir, highlighting their dosages and therapeutic alternatives.

3. **Medicines for HIV-Related Opportunistic Infections**: Listing of medicines like isoniazid and sulfamethoxazole for preventing opportunistic infections in HIV patients.

4. **Other Antivirals**: Inclusion of antivirals like ribavirin and valganciclovir for treating viral hemorrhagic fevers and cytomegalovirus retinitis, respectively.

5. **Antihepatitis Medicines**: Coverage of medicines for hepatitis B and C, including nucleoside/nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitors and pangenotypic direct-acting antivirals.

6. **Antiprotozoal Medicines**: Discussion of antiamoebic, antileishmaniasis, and antimalarial medicines, emphasizing the need for combination therapies and the development of new formulations.

Overall, the document serves as a comprehensive guide for essential medicines, emphasizing their importance in treating various infectious diseases and the need for ongoing development and testing of new therapies.

nodes.title: Antimalarial medicines
nodes.summary:
The partial document outlines the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines for 2023, specifically focusing on antiprotozoal medicines. It details various categories of antiprotozoal treatments, including:

1. **Antiamoebic and Antigiardiasis Medicines**: Lists medications such as diloxanide and metronidazole, along with their forms and dosages.

2. **Antileishmaniasis Medicines**: Describes treatments like amphotericin B, meglumine antimoniate, and miltefosine, highlighting the preference for liposomal formulations due to better safety profiles.

3. **Antimalarial Medicines**: Divided into curative treatments and chemoprevention, it emphasizes the use of combination therapies for P. falciparum malaria, recommending specific drug combinations and formulations, including artemether, artesunate, and chloroquine.

4. **Antipneumocystosis and Antitoxoplasmosis Medicines**: Lists medications such as pyrimethamine and sulfadiazine, along with various formulations.

5. **Antitrypanosomal Medicines**: Focuses on treatments for African trypanosomiasis, including fexinidazole for both stages of the disease and other medications like pentamidine and suramin sodium for specific infections.

The document emphasizes the importance of combination therapies, local availability, and safety profiles in the selection of these essential medicines.

The partial document outlines the 23rd List of Essential Medicines by the WHO for 2023, focusing on various treatments for specific diseases. Key points include:

1. **Medicines for African Trypanosomiasis**: It lists eflornithine and melarsoprol for treating Trypanosoma brucei gambiense infection, along with nifurtimox as a combination therapy.

2. **American Trypanosomiasis**: Benznidazole and nifurtimox are included for treatment.

nodes.title: Supportive medicines
nodes.summary:
The partial document outlines the 23rd List of Essential Medicines by the WHO for 2023, detailing various medications and their formulations, primarily focusing on treatments for different types of cancers and supportive therapies. Key points include:

1. **Cancer Treatments**: The document lists several essential medicines for treating various malignancies, including dexamethasone, hydrocortisone, leuprorelin, methylprednisolone, prednisolone, and tamoxifen, along with their specific indications such as acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, breast cancer, and multiple myeloma.

2. **Supportive Medicines**: It includes supportive treatments like allopurinol, mesna, rasburicase, and zoledronic acid, which are used for managing complications associated with cancer, such as tumour lysis syndrome and malignancy-related bone disease.

3. **Therapeutic Foods**: The document mentions ready-to-use therapeutic foods designed for the management of severe acute malnutrition, adhering to UN guidelines.

4. **Antianaemia Medicines**: It covers medicines affecting blood, particularly antianaemia treatments like ferrous salts, folic acid, and hydroxocobalamin, including their formulations and specific uses, such as supplementation during pregnancy.

5. **Coagulation Medicines**: The document also references medicines affecting coagulation, specifically dabigatran and its therapeutic alternatives, which are used for managing blood coagulation disorders.

Overall, the document serves as a comprehensive guide to essential medicines for cancer treatment, supportive care, nutritional needs, and blood-related therapies.

nodes.title: Antihypertensive medicines

It details antiarrhythmic medicines, antihypertensive medicines, and medications used in heart failure, providing specific drug names, dosages, and therapeutic alternatives. Key antiarrhythmic drugs mentioned include bisoprolol, digoxin, and epinephrine, while antihypertensive options include amlodipine, bisoprolol, and enalapril, among others. The document also highlights the use of certain medications, such as hydralazine and methyldopa, specifically for pregnancy-related hypertension. Additionally, it covers medicines for heart failure, including bisoprolol, digoxin, and furosemide, and lists antithrombotic medicines, including anti-platelet and thrombolytic agents. The document emphasizes the importance of these medications in managing cardiovascular conditions and provides guidance on their use and alternatives.

nodes.title: Antithrombotic medicines
nodes.summary:
The partial document outlines the 23rd List of Essential Medicines by the WHO for 2023, focusing on various categories of medications used primarily for heart failure, antithrombotic treatments, lipid-lowering agents, and dermatological medicines. Key points include:

1. **Heart Failure Medications**: Lists essential medicines such as bisoprolol, digoxin, enalapril, furosemide, hydrochlorothiazide, losartan, and spironolactone, along with their therapeutic alternatives and available formulations (tablets, injections, oral liquids).

2. **Antithrombotic Medicines**: Covers anti-platelet medicines like acetylsalicylic acid and clopidogrel, as well as thrombolytic agents such as alteplase and streptokinase, including their forms and dosages.

3. **Lipid-Lowering Agents**: Highlights simvastatin and its alternatives, indicating its use for high-risk patients.

4. **Fixed-Dose Combinations**: Describes combinations for the prevention of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, detailing various formulations that include acetylsalicylic acid, atorvastatin, ramipril, and other antihypertensive agents.

5. **Dermatological Medicines**: Lists antifungal treatments like miconazole, terbinafine, and others, specifying their forms and concentrations.

Overall, the document serves as a comprehensive guide to essential medicines for specific health conditions, emphasizing their therapeutic alternatives and available formulations.

The partial document outlines the 23rd List of Essential Medicines by the WHO for 2023, focusing on medications for diabetes, hypoglycemia, thyroid disorders, pituitary hormone system disorders, and immunologicals. Key points include:

1. **Diabetes Medications**: 
   - Insulins (soluble, intermediate-acting, long-acting analogues) with specific formulations and quality-assured biosimilars.
   - Oral hypoglycemic agents such as empagliflozin, gliclazide, and metformin, including therapeutic alternatives and dosage forms.

2. **Hypoglycemia Treatments**: 
   - Glucagon and diazoxide listed as treatments for hypoglycemia.

3. **Thyroid Hormones and Antithyroid Medicines**: 
   - Levothyroxine, potassium iodide, methimazole, and propylthiouracil, with specific indications and alternatives.

4. **Pituitary Hormone System Disorders**: 
   - Cabergoline and bromocriptine as treatments, along with octreotide for specific conditions.

5. **Immunologicals**: 
   - Diagnostic agents like tuberculin, and various sera, immunoglobulins, and monoclonal antibodies, including anti-rabies and diphtheria antitoxins, with compliance to WHO standards.

The document emphasizes the importance of quality assurance and provides detailed formulations and therapeutic alternatives for each category of medicines.

WHO immunization policy recommendations are published in vaccine position papers based on  recommendations made by the 
Strategic Advisory Group of Experts on Immunization (SAGE).   
WHO vaccine position papers are updated three to four times per year. The list be low details the vaccines for which there is a 
recommendation from SAGE and a corresponding WHO  position paper as at March 2023 . The  most recent version s of the WHO 
position papers, reflecting the current evidence related to a specific vaccine and the relat ed recommendations, can be accessed at 
any time on the WHO website at:  
https://www.who.int/teams/immunization -vaccines -and-biologicals/policies/position -papers   
Vaccine recommendations may be universal or conditional (e.g., in certain regions, in some high -risk populations or as part of 
immunization programmes with certain characteristics). Details are available in the  relevant position papers, and in the  Summary Tables 
of WHO Routine Immunization Recommendations available on  the WHO website at:  
https://www.who.int/teams/immunization -vaccines -and-biologicals/policies/who -recomme ndations -for-routine -immunization ---

Additionally, it covers ovulation inducers, uterotonics, antioxytocics (tocolytics), and other medicines administered to mothers and neonates. The document specifies the formulations, dosages, and therapeutic alternatives for each medicine, emphasizing their roles in reproductive health management, maternal care, and neonatal support.

structure.title: PERITONEAL DIALYSIS SOLUTION
structure.summary:
The partial document outlines the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines for 2023, specifically focusing on various medicines administered to mothers and neonates, as well as those for mental and behavioral disorders. Key points include:

1. **Medicines for Mothers**: 
   - Dexamethasone and a multiple micronutrient supplement containing essential vitamins and minerals such as Vitamin A, C, D, E, B vitamins, Iron, Iodine, Zinc, Selenium, and Copper.
   - Tranexamic acid for injection.

2. **Medicines for Neonates**: 
   - Caffeine citrate for injection and oral liquid.
   - Chlorhexidine solution or gel for umbilical cord care.
   - Surfactant for intratracheal instillation.

3. **Medicines for Mental and Behavioral Disorders**: 
   - Psychotic disorders: Includes fluphenazine, haloperidol, olanzapine, paliperidone, and risperidone, along with their therapeutic alternatives.
   - Mood disorders: Covers medicines for depressive disorders (e.g., amitriptyline, fluoxetine) and bipolar disorders (e.g., carbamazepine, lithium carbonate, quetiapine).

The document also mentions complementary lists and therapeutic alternatives for various medications.

nodes.title: Medicines for anxiety disorders
nodes.summary:
The partial document outlines the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines for 2023, specifically focusing on medications for various mental health and substance use disorders. Key points include:

1. **Valproic Acid**: Caution against use in pregnancy due to risks of birth defects and developmental disorders.
2. **Anxiety Disorders**: Lists medications such as diazepam for short-term management and fluoxetine with several therapeutic alternatives for longer-term treatment.
3. **Obsessive-Compulsive Disorders**: Includes clomipramine and fluoxetine, along with alternative medications.
4. **Substance Use Disorders**: 
   - **Alcohol Use Disorders**: Mentions acamprosate and naltrexone.
   - **Nicotine Use Disorders**: Lists bupropion, various forms of nicotine replacement therapy (NRT), and varenicline.

The document provides specific formulations and dosages for each medication mentioned.

 WHO Model List of Essential Medicines – 23rd List (2023) page 62 Table 1.2: Explanation of dosage forms  
 
A. Principal dosage forms used in EML – oral administration  
 
 
Term  
  
Definition  
 
Solid oral dosage form  Refers to tablets or capsules or other solid dosage forms such as 'melts' 
that are immediate -release preparations. It implies that there is no 
difference in clinical efficacy or safety between the available dosage forms, 
and countries should therefore choose the form(s) to be listed depending 
on quality and availability.   
 
The term 'solid oral dosage form' is never  intended to allow any type of 
modified -release tablet.  
 
Tablets  Refers to:  
 
• uncoated or coated (film -coated or sugar -coated) tablets that are 
intended to be swallowed whole;  
• unscored and scored*;  
• tablets that are intended to be chewed before being swallowed;  
• tablets that are intended to be dispersed or dissolved in water or 
another suitable liquid before being swallowed;  
• tablets that are intended to be crushed before being swallowed.  
 
The term 'tablet' without qualification is never  intended to allow any type of 
modified -release tablet.  
 
Tablets (qualified)  Refers to a specif ic type of tablet:  
chewable  - tablets that are intended to be chewed before being swallowed;  
dispersible - tablets that are intended to be dispersed in water or another 
suitable liquid before being swallowed;  
soluble - tablets that are intended to be dis solved in water or another 
suitable liquid before being swallowed;  
crushable  - tablets that are intended to be crushed before being 
swallowed;  
scored - tablets bearing a break mark or marks where sub -division is 
intended in order to provide doses of less than one tablet;  
sublingual  - tablets that are intended to be placed beneath the tongue.  
 
The term 'tablet' is always qualified with an additional term (in parentheses) 
in entries where one of the following types of tablet is intended: gastro -
resistant (such tablets may sometimes be described as enteric -coated or 
as delayed -release), prolonged -release or another modified -release form.  
  
 
* Scored tablets may be divided for ease of swallowing, provided that dose is a whole number of tablets.

structure.text:
WHO Model List of Essential Medicines  – 23rd List (202 3)  
 WHO Model List of Essential Medicines – 23rd List (2023) page 62 Table 1.2: Explanation of dosage forms  
 
A. Principal dosage forms used in EML – oral administration  
 
 
Term  
  
Definition  
 
Solid oral dosage form  Refers to tablets or capsules or other solid dosage forms such as 'melts' 
that are immediate -release preparations. It implies that there is no 
difference in clinical efficacy or safety between the available dosage forms, 
and countries should therefore choose the form(s) to be listed depending 
on quality and availability.   
 
The term 'solid oral dosage form' is never  intended to allow any type of 
modified -release tablet.  
 
Tablets  Refers to:  
 
• uncoated or coated (film -coated or sugar -coated) tablets that are 
intended to be swallowed whole;  
• unscored and scored*;  
• tablets that are intended to be chewed before being swallowed;  
• tablets that are intended to be dispersed or dissolved in water or 
another suitable liquid before being swallowed;  
• tablets that are intended to be crushed before being swallowed.  
 
The term 'tablet' without qualification is never  intended to allow any type of 
modified -release tablet.  
 
Tablets (qualified)  Refers to a specif ic type of tablet:  
chewable  - tablets that are intended to be chewed before being swallowed;  
dispersible - tablets that are intended to be dispersed in water or another 
suitable liquid before being swallowed;  
soluble - tablets that are intended to be dis solved in water or another 
suitable liquid before being swallowed;  
crushable  - tablets that are intended to be crushed before being 
swallowed;  
scored - tablets bearing a break mark or marks where sub -division is 
intended in order to provide doses of less than one tablet;  
sublingual  - tablets that are intended to be placed beneath the tongue.  
 
The term 'tablet' is always qualified with an additional term (in parentheses) 
in entries where one of the following types of tablet is intended: gastro -
resistant (such tablets may sometimes be described as enteric -coated or 
as delayed -release), prolonged -release or another modified -release form.  
  
 
* Scored tablets may be divided for ease of swallowing, provided that dose is a whole number of tablets.  WHO Model List of Essential Medicines  – 23rd List (202 3)  
 WHO Model List of Essential Medicines – 23rd List (2023) page 63 Capsules  Refers to hard or soft capsules.  
 
The term 'capsule' without qualification is  never  intended to allow any type 
of modified -release capsule.  
 
Capsules (qualified)  The term 'capsule' with qualification refers to gastro -resistant  (such 
capsules may sometimes be described as enteric -coated  or as  delayed -
release), prolonged -release  or another modified -release form.  
 
Granules  Preparations that are issued to patient as granules to be swallowed without 
further preparation, to be chewed, or to be taken in or with water or 
another suitable liquid.  
 
The term 'granules' without further qualification is never  intended to allow 
any type of modified -release granules.  
 
Oral powder  Preparations that are issued to patient as powder (usually as single -dose) 
to be taken in or with water or another suitable liquid.  
 
Oral liquid  Liquid preparations intended to be swallowed  i.e. oral solutions, 
suspensions, emulsions and oral drops, including those constituted from 
powders or granules, but not those preparations intended for oromucosal 
administration e.g. gargles and mouthwashes.  
 
Oral liquids presented as powders or granules may offer benefits in the 
form of better stability and lower transport costs. If more than one type of 
oral liqui d is available on the same market (e.g. solution, suspension, 
granules for reconstitution), they may be interchanged and in such cases 
should be bioequivalent. It is preferable that oral liquids do not contain 
sugar and that solutions for children do not c ontain alcohol.  
 
 
B. Principal dosage forms used in EML – parenteral administration  
 
Term  Definition  
Injection  Refers to solutions, suspensions and emulsions including those constituted 
from powders or concentrated solutions.  
Injection (qualified)  Route of administration is indicated in parentheses where relevant.  
Injection (oily)  The term `injection’ is qualified by `(oily)’ in relevant entries.  
Intravenous infusion  Refers to solutions and emulsions including those constituted from po wders 
or concentrated solutions.  
 
C. Other dosage forms  
 
Mode of administration  Term to be used  
To the eye  Eye drops, eye ointments.  
Topical  For liquids: lotions, paints.  
For semi -solids: cream, ointment.  
Rectal  Suppositories, gel or solution.  
Vaginal  Pessaries or vaginal tablets.  
Inhalation  Powder for inhalation, pressurized inhalation, nebulizer.
